svg.title: IP Source Guard depends on a binding table it does not build itself, and three host types that break it
svg.desc: Top: the chain. DHCP snooping watches the exchange between client and server and records a binding of port, MAC, address, VLAN and lease time; IP Source Guard then filters every data packet against that table, dropping any packet whose source address is not the one leased on that port. The important consequence: the filtering is only as good as the table, and the table only knows about hosts that used DHCP. Middle: three host types. A DHCP client works with no extra configuration. A static-address host is dropped until a static binding is entered by hand - the classic symptom is a printer or a building management controller that works until the day snooping is enabled. A server with a reservation still needs the lease in the table, and a moved cable needs a moved binding. Bottom: four failure modes. The binding table is empty because snooping was enabled on the server-facing port instead of the client-facing ones. The static bindings were never created, so the affected hosts go dark with no log anywhere. The lease expires while the host keeps the address. And the untrusted port carries a DHCP server the team forgot about, which poisons the table. A footer says the design question is not whether to enable it, but who maintains the static bindings and how a new static host gets one.
svg.text: IP Source Guard is only as strong as a table somebody else built
It does not discover addresses. It enforces a binding list, and the binding list only knows about DHCP.
client
DHCP Discover
DHCP snooping
watches the exchange
binding table
port · MAC · IP · VLAN · lease
IP Source Guard
filters data against the table
forward or drop
wrong source = silent drop
THREE HOST TYPES, THREE OUTCOMES
DHCP client
works with no extra configuration
the lease creates the binding, the
binding permits the traffic
this is the population the design assumes
Static-address host
dropped until a static binding is added
printers, cameras, building controllers,
anything the vendor fixed at the factory
works until the day snooping is enabled
Server with a reservation
still needs the lease in the table
a reservation is a promise about the
address, not an entry in the binding list
a moved cable needs a moved binding
FOUR WAYS THE TABLE LIES
1 snooping enabled on the server-facing port instead of the client ports - the table stays empty and everything is dropped
2 static bindings never created - the affected hosts go dark with no log line anywhere to explain it
3 the lease expires while the host keeps using the address - works, then stops, then works again
4 an unauthorised DHCP server on an untrusted port - the table is poisoned by design, and the gateway moves
The real design question is not whether to enable it, but who maintains the static bindings and what the workflow is when a new fixed-address device arrives.
Roll it out in this order: enable snooping with the server port trusted, watch the table populate for a week, then enable source guard on one access switch and let the tickets name the static hosts.
Export the static bindings to the same repository as the golden configuration. A binding that lives only in the switch is lost with the switch.
If the site has a large fixed-address population, say so before the project starts - it changes the estimate from weeks to months.
